title: Olive Oil Ramp
subject: Torts
stem:
Lydia operates a private, for-profit Bible-themed candle-dipping studio called Lampstand Studio. A statute requires businesses that invite the public into hands-on workshops to keep their customer walkway reasonably safe. Before opening for a paid “Psalms and Candles” class, Lydia hires Barnabas, an outside floor-care contractor, to cover and clean a slick olive-oil spill on the only ramp customers use to enter the studio. Barnabas negligently leaves the slick oil on the ramp, and Peter slips and falls while entering.

Call: What is Peter’s best argument against Lampstand Studio?
call: What is Peter's best argument against Lampstand Studio?

choices.A: Lampstand Studio is liable only if Lydia or one of her employees personally poured the oil on the ramp.
choices.B: Lampstand Studio has no possible liability because it hired an outside company to make the ramp safe.
choices.C: Lampstand Studio may be liable because the public-walkway safety duty is nondelegable.
choices.D: Lampstand Studio is liable because every outside company that works at a public business is treated as the business's employee.

rightExplanation: C is the best answer. It ties the claim to the fact that the business had the walkway-safety duty in the first place. Gold Key: when the law imposes a nondelegable safety duty on a hirer, the hirer may remain responsible even though an independent contractor performed the negligent work. Silver Key: do not turn this array into “contractor equals employee” or “contractor means no liability.” Look for the middle route: the duty stays with the business.

c3.label: CUT D
c3.text: “every outside company” is an absolute. That answer overconverts contractors into employees.

c3.label: CUT B
c3.text: “no possible liability” pushes the independent-contractor default too far. The Gold Key blocks the contractor-shield trap.

c3.label: CUT A
c3.text: “only if personally poured the oil” invents a personal-creation prerequisite. The Gold Key blocks the personal-act-only trap.

c3.label: Residual
c3.text: C remains. No CLASH or CALL is needed after the anchor-assisted CUT.

studentScript: Statutory safety duty. Outside contractor. Customer falls. Cut 'every contractor is employee.' Cut 'no possible liability.' Cut 'only if personally made the hazard.' Gold Key: nondelegable duty stays with the hirer. Pick C.

A.signal: The answer invents an 'only if the business personally made the hazard' route.
A.lawyer: A nondelegable duty may keep liability with the hirer even when the independent contractor created or failed to remove the hazard.

B.signal: The answer says 'no possible liability,' which pushes the independent-contractor default too far.
B.lawyer: Independent-contractor status is a default shield, not a complete shield when a nondelegable duty applies.

C.signal: The answer matches the statutory safety-duty trigger and uses the cautious 'may be liable' wording.
C.lawyer: Restatement (Second) of Torts § 424 supports liability where a statutory safety duty is breached by a contractor's failure to provide required precautions.

D.signal: The word 'every' is too broad; it converts all outside companies into employees.
D.lawyer: Nondelegable duty is not the same as employee status or respondeat superior.

goldKeys.statement: A statutory or otherwise nondelegable safety duty stays with the hirer even when the negligent work is done by an independent contractor.
goldKeys.trigger: statutory/public safety duty plus outside contractor

silverKeys.statement: When the stem gives a legal safety duty and an outside contractor, do not choose the all-or-nothing contractor answers; look for the duty-stays-with-the-hirer route.
silverKeys.trigger: statutory duty + hired contractor + injured public entrant

remediation.title: Independent contractor is not the end of the story
remediation.signal: Hirer has a statutory/public safety duty and hires someone else to perform it.
remediation.studentMove: Ask whether the duty itself can be delegated.
remediation.tinyRule: Nondelegable duty can keep liability with the hirer.
